summary: Specifies a Telnet option for passing environment information from a client to a server, so a user can carry configuration settings to a remote host when connecting.

plainLanguage.summary: When you visit a friend, you tell them your preferences. This lets a Telnet user pass settings to the computer they are visiting.

questions: what is the telnet environment option
how to send environment variables over telnet
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets a client pass environment variables such as USER and DISPLAY to the server at connection time.

tldr.problem: Operating systems keep startup information in environment variables that should follow a user to a remote machine, and creating a new Telnet option for each new piece of information would be wasteful.
tldr.mechanism: The NEW-ENVIRON option (code 39) lets the two sides negotiate with WILL and DO, then the side that sent DO asks for variables with SEND and the other side answers with IS, using VAR, VALUE, ESC and USERVAR markers.
tldr.outcome: One generic option carries any variable, with a set of well known names defined, and the server decides which variables to use. The RFC corrects errors in RFC 1408.

today: RFC 1572 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It corrects errors in RFC 1408; RFC 1571 covers interoperability with earlier implementations.

sections.title: Why a Generic Environment Option
sections.content:
Many operating systems have startup information and environment variables that should be passed to remote machines when Telnet connections are made. Rather than create a new Telnet option each time someone needs some new information carried through a session, this generic option can be used.

The RFC is an edited version of an earlier specification. It corrects some errors in RFC 1408, which had incorrectly reversed the values for VAR and VALUE and so disagreed with existing implementations. To fix this, a new option number was assigned to NEW-ENVIRON, which lets implementations of this memo interoperate without ambiguity.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of inventing a new special note every time, there is one general envelope that can carry any setting. An older version got two labels swapped, so this one fixes that.

sections.title: Commands and Codes
sections.content:
The option is called NEW-ENVIRON and has code 39. Inside a subnegotiation there are three commands: IS (0), SEND (1) and INFO (2). Four markers structure the data: VAR (0), VALUE (1), ESC (2) and USERVAR (3).

The usual Telnet negotiation applies. IAC WILL NEW-ENVIRON says the sender is willing to send environment variables, and IAC DO NEW-ENVIRON says it is willing to receive them. WONT and DONT refuse. The default is WONT and DONT, meaning no environment information is exchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of message and label has a small number, like a code word. By default nobody sends any settings unless both sides agree.

sections.title: SEND, IS and INFO
sections.content:
Only the side that sent DO NEW-ENVIRON may start a SEND. It lists variables by type, either VAR for well known names or USERVAR for user defined names. If no list is given, the default environment of both kinds should be sent. A type with no name means all variables of that type.

Only the side that sent WILL NEW-ENVIRON may answer with IS. The answers must come back in the same order as requested, with a response for each type explicitly requested. A type not followed by VALUE means the variable is undefined. A VALUE followed directly by a type or IAC means it is defined but empty.

A client may reply with an empty environment, IAC SB NEW-ENVIRON IS IAC SE, when nothing is defined. The INFO command has the same format as IS but is for propagating changes, and may be sent spontaneously. It is not to be used for the initial information.

If data contains IAC it must be sent as IAC IAC. If a name or value contains VAR, USERVAR, VALUE or ESC, it must be preceded by ESC.
sections.plainLanguage: The host asks 'what are your settings?' and the visitor answers with a list of names and values. If something in the list looks like a label, it gets a special mark so it is not mixed up.

sections.title: Well Known Variables
sections.content:
The RFC defines these well known variables, sent with type VAR:

  • USER: the account name the client wants to log into.
  • JOB: the job ID to use when logging in.
  • ACCT: the account ID to use when logging in.
  • PRINTER: the default location for printer output; its format is undefined.
  • SYSTEMTYPE: the operating system type, with the same value as the FTP SYSTEM (SYST) command.
  • DISPLAY: the X display location, in the form <host>:<dispnum>[.<screennum>].

For DISPLAY, if it conflicts with the Telnet X-DISPLAY-LOCATION option, the most recently received information should be used. The USERVAR type carries arbitrary pairs. It lets implementations tell values derived by the remote host software from values supplied by the user, though paranoid implementations will probably distrust both equally.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a short list of common settings, like your name, your account and where to show windows. Anything else can go in as a custom setting.

sections.title: Implementation Rules
sections.content:
WILL and DO are used only at the beginning of the connection to obtain and grant permission. After that the DO side is free to request variables. The option may be used at any time, but exchange usually happens at startup because many operating systems can only propagate environment information when a process is created, so it is needed before the user logs in.

The receiving host need not put every received variable in the environment. It may ignore a TERM variable if the terminal type is already known from the TERMINAL-TYPE option, or use USER, ACCT and PROJ to choose an account without putting them in the environment. Putting all unknown information into the user's environment is the suggested method, because it gives the user the most flexibility. Any implementation that supports NEW-ENVIRON is expected to support all of this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The host does not have to accept every setting. It can skip ones it already knows, but the best plan is to keep unfamiliar ones so the visitor has the most freedom.

sections.title: Security Concerns
sections.content: Implementors need to understand how setting variables interacts with login and authentication. Careful analysis should decide which variables are safe to set before the client has logged in. A bad choice would be to allow a variable to be changed that lets an intruder circumvent or compromise the login or authentication program itself.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger could change any setting before proving who they are, they might trick the door guard. So the host must choose carefully which settings to allow.

messages.label: SB NEW-ENVIRON SEND VAR "USER" VAR "ACCT" VAR USERVAR SE
messages.note: Asks for USER, ACCT and the default sets.

messages.label: SB NEW-ENVIRON IS VAR "USER" VALUE "joe" ... SE
messages.note: Returns the variables with their values.
